title: Food, reflected on
hook: one of the forty subjects asks you to like your lunch less. why?
tomorrow: what is your body actually made of?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young man walked away from the quietest state his teacher knew. Not the end. Today, something much less lofty: lunch.

A sandwich in one hand, a phone in the other, gone before you tasted it. So what does a meditation manual have to say about lunch? Something odd. In Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, one of the forty meditation subjects is the perception of repulsiveness in food. Practice finding your meal unappealing. That's a strange thing to ask of anyone, let alone someone who has just been handed it as a gift. Why would a monk train himself to like his lunch less?
screen: `A SANDWICH, A PHONE, GONE.` → `ONE SUBJECT: REPULSIVENESS IN FOOD.` → `WHY LIKE YOUR LUNCH LESS?`

segments.voice: Buddhaghosa's answer is a journey. He walks the monk through the whole life of one meal. Leaving the quiet of the monastery, in heat or cold. Walking to the village. Going house to house with a bowl, past dogs and puddles. Then the chewing, the swallowing, the stomach, and finally where it leaves the body. Nothing on that list is false. It's food's whole trip, not just the picture of it on a plate. And the target isn't the food. It's the craving. As the perception grows, the manual says, the mind draws back from the hunger for flavors, and the monk eats just to keep going, without fuss or vanity. There's an older reflection behind this, in the Buddha's discourse on all the taints, chanted before meals in monasteries: I use this food not for fun, not for showing off, not to bulk up or to look good, but to keep this body going, to ease hunger's discomfort, and to support the good life. So the puzzle comes apart. The strange meditation isn't hate for your lunch. It's seeing the meal whole, field to body, so the grabbing loosens and the eating becomes plain, and even grateful.
screen: `FOLLOW ONE MEAL ALL THE WAY.` · `NOTHING ON THE LIST IS FALSE.` · `THE TARGET IS THE CRAVING.` · `NOT FOR FUN, BUT TO KEEP GOING.` · then, large: `FOOD'S JOURNEY.`

segments.voice: Take the last thing you ate and follow it backward: the field or the orchard, the hands that picked it, the truck, the store, your own hands. Then follow it forward, into your body, becoming the next hour of your day. Keep it plain, no judging, just the trip.
Food, reflected on: one of the forty subjects. A meal seen on its whole journey, so it's eaten to keep going, not to feed the craving.
For the road: food's journey, longer than the minutes it spends on the plate. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics recite a reflection on the purpose of food, drawn from the Discourse on All the Taints, before or while eating; the perception of repulsiveness in food is a meditation subject in the Visuddhimagga, taken up with a teacher.

it follows the meal's whole trip so the craving for flavors loosens. the food isn't the enemy.
Buddhaghosa follows the meal all the way through the body
from the walk to the village to the stomach and beyond. nothing on the list is false.
the reflection says to eat for pleasure and good looks
it says the opposite: not for fun, not to look good, but to keep the body going and support the good life.

fork.setup: a friend says she's trying a meditation that makes her feel guilty every time she enjoys a meal. what would Buddhaghosa's practice say?
options: guilt is the point: the more you dislike food, the better.
the point is loosening craving, not guilt; eat plainly, even gladly.
skip it: meditation shouldn't touch something as ordinary as food.
fork.reveal: the target is craving for flavors, not the meal and not the eater. the monk eats to keep going, without fuss.

original.note: Pali: perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, one of the forty meditation subjects.

trapdoor: what you thought: a meditation for hating your food.
what it means: following a meal's whole journey so craving for flavors loosens and eating becomes plain.

what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga 11 lists the aspects (going, seeking, using, digestion, excretion and more); the reflection on food's purpose comes from Majjhima Nikaya 2, the Discourse on All the Taints.
guess: a meal seen on its whole trip, eaten without craving
a strict diet that cuts out every tasty dish
a fast kept to make the mind sharp and light
recall: the subtlest calm, and still not the end
resting on the thought: there is nothing

chat.meaning: The practice follows food's whole journey so craving loosens. The monk eats to keep going: not a race, not a feast.

tie.story: Buddhaghosa follows one meal from the village to the body, so the craving loosens.
tie.friend: Mai can take her lunch break as a meal, not a race.

Buddhaghosa.meaning: the commentator who wrote the Path of Purification

the taints.meaning: the deep stains of the mind a discourse teaches how to end

monastery.meaning: where monks or nuns live, study and practice together

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 11 (the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment: the aspects of going, seeking, using, secretion, receptacle, the uncooked and cooked, fruit, outflow and smearing; as it grows the mind retreats from craving for flavors and he uses nutriment only to cross over suffering, without vanity)

Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (wisely reflecting, he uses almsfood not for amusement, intoxication, adornment or beautification, but for the endurance of this body, ending discomfort and assisting the holy life)

notes: Visuddhimagga 11 and MN 2 paraphrased. Confirm the summary of the aspects (the 'dogs and puddles' detail stands in for the manual's description of the alms walk) and of MN 2's reflection on food.
'Chanted before meals in monasteries': the paccavekkhana reflection is recited in Theravada monasteries; confirm the wording is fair without claiming every monastery.
Puzzle shape: the odd detail is a meditation on finding food unappealing; the answer is that the target is craving, not the meal.
The outline says 'from field to body'; the Visuddhimagga's aspects begin at the monastery door, so the field appears in the practice and the teach's last line.
